title: Fire Burning in My Head
abstract: Written by a professor of clinical psychology, this book is accessible to thoughtful readers interested in the relation between spirituality and mental disorders. It comprises two main parts: The first part tells the story of how a psychologist-cum-patient performs a self-study of "madness" in great detail. It belongs to the long tradition of ideographic studies that attend to the uniqueness of each individual. The author says: "During episodes, manic symptoms are manifest. Yet, I become more colorful, sensitive, generous, and loving. I see beauty everywhere and delight in the simple things of life. I glimpse into mystical magnanimity. All these inform me that my quest for spirituality is wedded to madness. Now, I can bear testimony that on balance the creative energy of madness may enrich rather than damage one’s life. It is possible to retain a measure of madness in dignified living and of dignity even in a state of madness." Adhering to the nomothetic tradition of knowledge generation, the second part gives extensive coverage to various aspects of mental disorders from a scientific perspective, including the ethical, political, and sociocultural contexts in which mental disorders occur. It resolves apparent contradictions between dualities, such as normality and abnormality, individualism and collectivism, and Eastern and Western values. In the end, the reader may learn that it is possible to harness the creative energy of madness to enrich one’s spiritual life—a topic that can hardly be found in psychiatric texts.

Short impact summary

Published in 2023 by Peter Lang Verlag, Fire Burning in My Head is a clinical psychology monograph that bridges spirituality and mental health through the author's introspective case study. The work engages substantively with questions of human dignity and social equity, aligning with efforts to reduce inequalities. While formal citation uptake remains nascent, the book has achieved modest institutional presence and demonstrates thematic relevance to policy frameworks addressing mental health disparities.

Full narrative

David Y. F. Ho's Fire Burning in My Head occupies a distinctive scholarly niche: written by a clinical psychologist reflecting on his own lived experience of mental illness, the work combines rigorous psychoanalytic and psychological frameworks with phenomenological self-examination. The dual-part structure—first presenting an in-depth ideographic study of manic episodes and their spiritual dimensions, then broadening to theoretical synthesis—situates the book within a long tradition of case-based learning in psychology while remaining accessible to educated lay readers concerned with mental health and spirituality.

The conceptual landscape mapped across the work spans spirituality, psychology, psychoanalysis, aesthetics, and dignity, with secondary engagement in sociology and epistemology. This thematic range reflects an effort to reintegrate the spiritual and the psychological—domains often treated separately in contemporary mental health discourse. The alignment with Sustainable Development Goal 5 (Reduced Inequalities) suggests implicit concern with access to dignified mental health care and the structural inequalities that shape how madness and spiritual experience are pathologized or valorized across different communities.

Formal scholarly reception is still forming. The work has not yet accumulated citations in indexed databases, a pattern common for recent monographs, particularly those published by university presses in the humanities and social sciences, where citation trajectories differ markedly from journal articles. The book holds modest library presence—three confirmed holdings in OpenLibrary institutions—indicating selective adoption in academic and research collections. The work is registered in the OpenAIRE repository, ensuring discoverability in the open research infrastructure.

The book's impact story remains early. No event data, media coverage, or secondary discourse analysis is currently recorded in available indices. However, the substantive engagement with dignity, spirituality, and psychological experience, combined with its clinical psychology authorship and accessibility to general readers, positions the work to contribute over time to conversations about mental health equity, the role of spirituality in recovery, and the integration of first-person knowledge in psychiatric and psychological scholarship.
